en: In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇīya*, such is the explanation of its own title.
"Vajra" (Diamond) is a metaphor for its nature. This nature is formless; once it falls into words, it is no longer itself.
The Master from India, having no choice but to speak, therefore named it *Prajñā* (Wisdom) and named it *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment).

Regarding the three types of *bodhi*, one might say that while the written words have become increasingly elaborate, their original essence was never manifold. Therefore, at the beginning of the sutra, these two characters—"Thus" (*evam*)—are brought forth.
"Thus" refers to the nature-body (*dharmatā-kāya*); it neither changes nor differs. How could it be something to be understood? How could it be something not to be understood?
Encountering a person of wisdom such as the venerable Subhūti, their profound capacities met, and the secret meanings were fully proclaimed.
He said: "Abide thus; thus subdue [the mind]. He further said: "Thus generate the pure mind. Regarding his discourse on giving, he said:
"One should give in this manner. Regarding his discourse on karmic retribution, he said: "Merit is likewise so. He required a person capable of understanding.
It is said: "To know thus, to see thus, and to believe and understand thus—this is to profoundly clarify the Buddha-dharma and to shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata.
Regarding such people, it is said: "They are no different from others. When praising the World-Honored One, it is said:
"Such a World-Honored One is no different from any other [object of veneration]. When their emotion reaches its peak and they shed tears, it is said: "To have heard such a sutra as this..."
This is a distinct teaching. Regarding the inconceivable wondrous wisdom of the thirty-two marks of reality (*dharmatā*): when words are exhausted, one forgets speech;

sitting upright in silence, one recites verses that amount to nothing more than saying, "Practice such contemplation. Thus we know that the fundamental essence of the *Vajra* is thus for the Buddhas of antiquity and the holy sages, and likewise for ordinary beings such as King Kali;
it is also thus for the city of King Prasenajit and the pagodas and temples as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
It is thus. Five hundred lifetimes before and five hundred lifetimes after—throughout incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka*) as well—it is no different.

Since the Patriarch of Huangmei first proclaimed the purport of the Sūtra, there have been more than eight hundred schools of interpretation; yet, as for those who have attained the intimate and direct path:

Only the Sixth Patriarch resolved this in a single word, saying: "The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent; it is called 'suchness' (tathatā). To say that all these are the Buddha-dharma is to be attached to them.
Judging by his intent, it was nothing more than using such a mind to expound such a sutra and to become such a Buddha.

I have held this sutra for twenty years, yet my oral recitations have been a mere superficial practice, and I have suffered in vain without attaining realization. It was only when I encountered the ashes of the kalpa and the shackles of the blade [of the sword]...
Sawing wood, cast into a remote wilderness and imprisoned, with but a single bundle by my side, I have maintained mindfulness of you in both dream and waking alike until my eventual return.
Having resided in the capital for another five years, I have now retrieved the text I recite and that which was previously entrusted to me;

I silently pondered the words of deliberation spoken by the Venerable Master during his nine-year confinement behind closed doors, as well as the verse left behind by Chan Master Xiying which I obtained while at Mount Huangbo. During these intervals since arriving in the capital...

At Changchun Temple, I listened to Master Yusheng’s exposition of the Dharma. I subsequently entered the Western Mountains to attend a vegetarian feast, where I recognized that his casual talk was entirely like gaining something and then losing it.
Thereupon, I closed my scroll and sat in stillness, contemplating the white text of the sutra; the *tathatā* essence leaped from the paper.
It had simply been hidden from view by the delusions of my habitual consciousness until now. I have recorded this as it came to hand, and after a long time, it has finally come forth.
This forms a volume. Although it may not necessarily coincide perfectly with such an original essence, the commentaries of the eight hundred masters do not do so either.
Yet, I wish to bring them all entirely into accord with this. This, too, is the nature of Suchness (tathatā), which vibrantly dwells within my own body;
it cannot be inherently different from that of a Tathāgata or an ordinary person. How could I not interpret it in this way? This is called [the Name].
By means of the name "prajñā," by means of "anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," the Buddha has already spoken much;
how much more so regarding the dharma that is non-abiding, signless, unattainable, and ineffable?

To seek it thus, to understand it thus—is it not to return from suchness to the absence of suchness, to return from thisness to the absence of thisness, and to return from understanding to the absence of understanding?
There is no understanding. I repent and confess this within myself, and for this reason I style myself the "Wayman Without Rightness.
This is the preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as interpreted by the Wayman Without Rightness, who has taken up residence in Mount Shijing.
When the First Patriarch Bodhidharma came from the West, he specifically praised the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as being capable of sealing the mind (*yinxin*).

Yet, in the end, it was not equal to the single-fascicle *Vajracchedikā*, which has constantly served as the seal of the mind. For this reason, the Fifth Patriarch of Huangmei first took the lead in promoting it and proclaiming its essential meaning;
those who subsequently provided commentaries numbered more than eight hundred schools. As for the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi, he initially attained realization through the text.
Later, he again used this to open his mouth and compose the *Platform Sutra*. He further concluded with a single word, saying: "The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent;
that which is called 'suchness'—all of it is the Buddha-dharma. One should know that regarding this sutra, the Buddha gave Subhūti one blow for every single phrase.
A single word, a single shout—language and written characters are eradicated without remainder.

This is the direct transmission outside the teachings, the primary meaning of the West’s arrival, which governs the life-force of the Buddhas and patriarchs. Among all the scriptures, it is honored as supreme and acclaimed as king; this is indeed to be believed.
There are three translations of this text preserved in the canon: those by Dharmaruci of the Northern Wei and Paramārtha of India during the Chen dynasty.
However, neither is as excellent as the translation by Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin; its phrasing is particularly concise and clear, and its meaning is free from omission or error.

Consequently, its recitation and study in China have flourished like the competing radiance of the sun and moon, yet the commentaries have branched into many schools with divergent views. Since my youth, at the age of twenty, I have been resolved...
Through study, he came to understand the convergence of the three teachings. In the year of Bingchen, due to a karmic affinity with the Master Liang, he took refuge in Master Hanshan.

On the day of his journey to the East, he received the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* for the Resolution of Doubts (*Jingang jueyi*), which he took as his guiding principle. Its general purport is as follows:
The Buddha taught the Dharma for thirty years, yet even his foremost disciples still harbored doubts.
This sutra follows the points of doubt raised by Kūṣaṇa (Kongsheng) and immediately refutes them; that is to say, "doubt and regret are forever exhausted, and one dwells securely within true wisdom.
Master Hanzhi manifested his physical body at Caoxi and was titled the Seventh Patriarch; he faced the Sixth Patriarch directly. Is this not being able to act according to one's capacity?

To expound [the Dharma] such that it truly accords with the mind-seal of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and simultaneously accords with the great purport of Confucius’s "One Thread" and the wordless [teaching], is nothing other than what Nanyue attained through the unimpeded wisdom of the *Vajracchedikā* and what Zhongfeng was able to do by using worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
More than forty years have passed since then; regarding the discourses heard and the writings seen during that interval:
Commentary: Those who have attempted to delineate the true face of this sutra are countless; yet, it is only through the interpretation of Master Tán that we are able to see it clearly.
This is like a mirror reflecting a mirror, where no forms remain; like light meeting light, where all dust is extinguished.
By simply upholding these four characters—*Evam mayā śrutam* (Thus have I heard)—one encompasses the entire sutra, and by extension, the entire Tripiṭaka. It is like water entering [the ocean].

Like milk or a mustard seed cast into a needle’s eye—Sanskrit and Chinese words brought together as they are picked up—extending this principle to all categories, there is no realm that is not harmonized.
Thus, the subtle refinements of Confucius and Mencius are set forth with full platter; the profound mysteries of Laozi and Zhuangzi are overturned to their very depths.

Every single point is realized as a family treasure, free from any artificial blending or conventional molds. This could not have been achieved were it not for one who was granted a great mandate and cast into the midst of peril and hardship.

Emerging from the balance of adversity through the practice of forbearance, how could one not radiate light equal to the *Ji-chou* (the Nine Categories of the Great Plan) and the *Qi-yi* (the Changes of Zhou)?

Furthermore, this is not merely the full manifestation of the religious teachings; it is the perfection of both merit and wisdom. Entering the mud and the water, one treads the path with ease and certainty.
How could one not possess the Vajra-eye and the Vajra-mind, acting as the Buddha’s mouth to proclaim the unsurpassed, most profound, and wondrous Truth, appearing before the Elder?
He preached the Dharma while manifesting in the body of a high official. To those with the true eye, he was known as a stainless one returned from the beyond (*anāgāmin*).
Upon re-examining the timing and circumstances, one’s faith will surely be further strengthened. This commentary was previously carved into woodblocks at the ancient monastery of Zhènghǎi in Wúmén.
Now it is being re-carved for inclusion in the Tripitaka and circulated through the Lénghuán Jīngfáng (Lengyan Sutra Monastery). It places the two venerable masters Zǐbó and Hǎnshān together.
Xiang Jiguang nodded in agreement. This is indeed a supreme cause spanning kalpas. An ancient worthy said: "Seeing and hearing serve as the seeds;
by transcending the eight difficulties, one surpasses the stages of the ten bhūmis. When understanding and practice are embodied, the fruit of vast kalpas is perfected in a single lifetime.

It is because Master Wushi held such an interpretation that he claimed that both the "Suchness" (Ruru) and the "Six Suchnesses" (Liu Ru) ultimately reduce to redundant meaning, and that the single character "Such" (Ru)— [The text provided ends abruptly.]
Nor should one take pleasure in hearing what is agreeable. This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) wherein the myriad dharmas come together yet not a single hair’s breadth remains attached.

Written on the eighth day of the twelfth month of the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era by the lay practitioner Tan Zhenmo (Dao-yi) of Xunli, respectfully composed as the Preface to the *Jingang Rushi Jie* (Commentary on the Suchness of the Diamond Sutra).
Divine power cannot be recorded in stone inscriptions; the vast ocean cannot be fathomed with a shell. The unsurpassed, wondrous Way cannot be explained through commentary;
it is precisely because it cannot be reached by commentary. Thus, though one speaks all day, there is no speaking;
though one leaves traces all day, there are no traces. Therefore, Kāśyapa said: "In forty-nine years, I have never uttered a single word. He further said: "But..."
There are verbal expressions that possess no real meaning whatsoever. They are like a bird-catcher whose intent lies in the bird; once the bird is caught, the trap is cast aside.

Or like a fisherman whose intent lies in the fish; once the fish is caught, the bait is discarded. If one were to cling to the bait or the trap as being the fish or the bird, this would not be the fault of the creator, but rather the ignorance of the person of the moment.

There was no such person as Zhang Gong. Having attained realization through his exhaustive study of the *Vajra*, he was unwilling to monopolize its subtleties for himself alone, desiring instead to share them with the world.
Amidst his efforts to serve his sovereign and benefit the people, he probed the profound and subtle mysteries and composed a commentary upon it, entitled the *Rushi jie* (Commentary on Suchness).
In the year Dingyou, while serving as a Regional Governor (*fangbo*) in Wulin, he produced the complete text and requested a preface. I have now examined it...
Having finished reading it, he looked back and said to his two or three disciples: "The sublime purport of the entire scripture is exhausted in these two characters.
Though other matters, such as the classification of chapters and phrases, may comprise more than several thousand words, they are nothing more than glosses upon these two characters.
As for those who have subsequently followed this text with sub-commentaries—whether from China or India, numbering no fewer than a thousand—they are, in essence, like analyzing emptiness."
Establishing boundaries, each party clings to their own private views; though emptiness is not something separate from them, they labor in vain.
Only Vasubandhu and Asaṅga established the principles and clarified the core tenets, shattering doubts and severing attachments, thereby attaining a penetration of the Buddha’s intent.

Yet even they could not entirely transcend the limitations of phrasing to point directly to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is the understanding that, once attained within the mind, does not rely on the tongue for its profound meaning.
To give form to these words is not to entrust my meaning to private attachments; it is like adding color within the darkness or carving patterns upon the surface of water.
There is this matter, though there is no fixed principle; one perceives it according to what one has attained. Its contribution to those whose learning is restricted is truly great!
I, a man of the mountains and fields, am incapable of elegant composition, yet since the Dharma does not change its essential function, I offer this "brocade" praise. However—
It is said: “The World-Honored One spoke thus; Master Wushi Gong understood thus; Master Shanye recorded thus.
These three ‘thus-nesses’ alone are like the sound of a poison-smeared drum—its resonance cannot be met—and like the edge of the Great A Sword—its point cannot be touched.”

Furthermore, it is like the cry of a crane amidst the clouds or the whistling of wind through a stone crevice; since these cannot be reconciled through logic, nor can they be interpreted through conceptual thought, those who read this sutra should simply take it as such.
They are immediately of one and the same adamantine nature with the speaker and the interpreter, and of one and the same non-abiding samādhi.
Why must one exhaustively count the characters, lines, names, and phrases before one finally believes in the non-existence [of inherent nature]?
This is the mark of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

Although it is certainly an error to mistake a baited pellet for a fish or a bird, if one were to obtain a single fish or a single bird and then desire to cause all people in the world to utterly abandon pellets and slingshots, I know that such a person is likewise insufficient to speak of the Way.
Did not the former sages say: "In the ground of the reality-limit..."?
To receive even a single speck of dust within the gateway of Buddha-activity is to not abandon a single dharma.

Thus, even if this sutra were proclaimed in every household and this interpretation transmitted through every door, it would simply be the place where the radiance of the true Vajra-seed is manifested. What harm could there be?
My humble preface is spoken thus as words of truth; it is speech that is neither deceptive nor false. Let those with the eye of discernment take it up.
The *Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra* entitled "Thus Explained" (*Rúshìjiě*),
composed by the Lingyin practitioner Hongli while residing at Shijing Mountain on the north bank of the Hebei River; annotated by the practitioner Wushi.

Within the assembly for the *Prajñāpāramitā*, Sun Bei-hai Cheng-ze of the capital, Xue Xing-wu of He-yang, and Zhang Tian-shi Ruo-qi of Jiao-zhou together read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
All five metals are called "gold. As for "Vajra," it is like the hard iron found in swords and blades; its hardness resides within the gold.
It is tempered a hundred times without being diminished; taking its hardness and sharpness, it can sever all things.
Just as wisdom (*prajñā*) can utterly sever greed, anger, delusion, and all inverted views—*prajñā* is a Sanskrit term meaning "wisdom" in the language of Tang (Chinese);
*pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term meaning "reaching the other shore. To reach the other shore, one must rely upon *prajñā*. *Sūtra* means a path.
It carries the Supreme Vehicle and leads one up the path to Bodhi. The *Vajra Preface* by Zen Master Dajian states:

"Gold exists within the mountain, yet the mountain does not know it is treasure; the treasure likewise does not know it is a mountain. This is because they lack sentience (*svabhāva*). Humans, however, possess sentience.
To obtain the treasure for use, the goldsmith breaks through the mountain to extract the ore and uses fire to smelt and refine it. Thus, [the essence] is obtained.
It becomes refined gold. The nature within the body of the four elements is likewise so. Within the world there is the mountain of self and person;

within this mountain of self and person there is the ore of afflictions; within the ore of afflictions there is the jewel of buddha-nature; within the jewel of buddha-nature there is the artisan of wisdom.
Using the fire of awakening to smelt and refine it, one beholds the diamond of one’s own nature, vividly clear and pure.
For this reason, the diamond (vajra) is used as a metaphor. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "It is like smelting gold ore;
the gold does not exist because of the smelting, yet although it is originally gold, it is ultimately through smelting that it is perfected.

One can thus know that the diamond does not fall into emptiness, for its refinement inherently possesses efficacy. This sūtra is also called the *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā*, and it constitutes the sixth part of the great [Prajñāpāramitā] collection.
Among the one hundred fascicles, the five hundred and seventy-seventh is titled the *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā*. This means that a single fascicle can encompass the meaning of the extensive version;
it is not that there are large and small versions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* itself. This sutra has been widely circulated in the world since the time of the Fifth Patriarch at Huangmei.
Wang Shizhen’s *Wanwei Yubian* records that during the time of Duke Mu of Qin, a stone Buddha was discovered in Fufeng.
The Duke did not recognize it and cast it away among filth. Later, he fell ill and dreamed of a celestial reprimand. When he questioned Youyu, Youyu replied:
"During the time of King Mu of Zhou, a transformed person arrived and said, 'This is the Buddha. The Divine King [Duke Mu] constructed for him the Zhongtian Terrace. Thereupon, the Duke...
He ordered Youyu to examine it. Youyu said, "This is truly a divine Buddha. The Duke offered him sacrifices of the three animals, but Youyu said, "The Buddha-dharma is pure;

for all offerings, one need only burn incense. The *Yijing tuji* (Record of the Translation of the Scriptures) states that Emperor Ming was moved by a miraculous dream and issued an edict to the Langzhong Cai Yin and others to welcome Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who brought the scriptures upon white horses.
The subsequent account states: "It is not correct to say that the Buddha-dharma first entered China during the Han dynasty.
*The First Division: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly.* Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly...

The Master was accompanied by a multitude of one thousand two hundred and fifty people. At that time, at the hour of eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location.
When he had finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.
"Thus have I heard": at the time of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, he instructed Ānanda that the phrase "Thus have I heard" should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras.
The Buddha is called "Awakened" (buddha) because he has awakened himself and awakened others; it is because his awakening is perfect. [The location is] Śrāvastī.
This is where King Prasenajit resided. "Jeta’s Grove" refers to that which was bestowed by Prince Jeta.

"Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden" refers to the garden of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, specifically the place where gold was spread over the ground. "Bhikṣu" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the language of China (Huayan), it means "mendicant.
[Such a person] "begs for the Dharma from the Buddhas above" and "begs for food among the people below. There were one thousand two hundred [monks].
Fifty people: the three Kāśyapas, Maudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and five other disciples; these numbers combined together.
These two characters, "Thus" (Evam), constitute the very marrow of the entire sutra. The Sixth Patriarch said: "The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent—this is called 'Thus' (Tathatā).
All that is the Buddha-Dharma is called 'Is' (Satya). Therefore, abiding is called 'abiding in Thusness,' and subduing is called 'subduing in Thusness.'"
This is subduing. Regarding giving, it says: "One gives in this manner. Regarding merit, it says: "Merit is likewise thus. Regarding purity, it says:
"In this manner one generates a pure mind. Furthermore, it says: "Thus knowing, thus seeing, thus believing and understanding.
Again, it says: "Suchness is immovable. Again, it says: "One should contemplate in this manner. In each case, the sharp points of their interaction were like those of a master and disciple.
When [the Buddha] threw [the flower], he said, "It is so, it is so. Confucius said, "Can one word govern one's life?
Is it not 'shu' (reciprocity)? Shu means "to accord with the mind" (*ru-xin*). Thus, Zengzi’s realization of the "One Thread" (*yiguan*) is also called "loyalty and shu" (*zhong-shu*).

Zisi’s "non-emergence" (*wei-fa*) and Mencius’s "immovability" (*bu-dong*) all share this same meaning. Therefore, the Sūtra says, "All phenomena have the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). As for "I have heard," I have indeed heard it.
Regarding the Buddha, one hears it from me as well. Ānanda, manifesting his physical presence, what is it that he hears?
What is it that he does not hear? "The patterns and writings of the Master can be heard. "At one time" refers to when [the Buddha] was in Wei;
"at that time" refers to when he entered the city. "Then," when the Elder Subhūti asked about the Dharma, was the time when the Dharma was being preached.
The Buddha-dharma manifests according to the occasion; this is what is meant by the "sage's timeliness. It is not confined to a single moment.
At all times, there is no time when it is not present. As for the Way, it cannot be departed from for even a brief instant.
Take, for example, the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī: therein one perceives the lands of atoms, where every blade of grass, tree, and pavilion is, point by point, the Reality.
It is thus: not only do I possess it, but all the great assembly of bhikṣus, all humans and devas, as well as beings of other species, share it together.
Confucius said: "There is no conduct of mine that I do not share with my disciples; this is what makes me 'Qiu' (the One).
Therefore, these one thousand two hundred and fifty people all possess this nature, all possess this prajñā, and thus all possess this Buddha-body. In the world...

The Venerable One transmitted his heart-mind to the assembly with this admonition: "Do not speak of it; the matter lies in the very act of putting on clothes and eating food. Seek its ultimate resolution there.
Therefore, when wearing robes and begging for alms, one is in no way different from others. This serves to humble my own pride and generate the merit of the donors.
Returning to the original place is merely borrowing words from the shadow; the original ground can be returned to, which is none other than one's own primordial nature.
He may return. When the meal is finished, the gathering up of the robes and bowl serves to represent the Buddha’s shedding of defilements and returning to the state of non-being.

Washing the feet likewise represents the cleansing of the dust of the mundane world. Spreading out his seat and sitting down signifies entering a state of tranquil meditation and attaining transformation.
For the true nature of Bodhi has no characteristics of entering or exiting, nor of going or returning.
The marks [of the Buddha] are neither identical with nor separate from the royal city of Śrāvastī; he proceeds through the streets begging for alms and returns to his original place.
Fundamentally, there is no duality of views. Upon arriving, he spreads his seat and sits; therein, the abiding mind and the subduing mind both reside.
This constitutes the second part, which prefigures the mechanism [of practice]. It must be understood by those capable of self-awakening.
A monk went to visit National Teacher Zhong. The Master asked him, "What is your occupation? The monk replied, "I lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The Master asked, "What are the first two characters? The monk said, "'Thus' (*evam*). The Master asked, "What is that?
The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Alas! With what do you lecture on the sutra?"
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "I beg for your instruction. Zhaozhou said, "Have you finished eating your congee?

The monk replied, "I have finished. Zhaozhou said, "Go wash your bowl. The monk attained great enlightenment. The Sixth Patriarch said, "The non-arising of mental thoughts is what is meant by 'sitting' (zuò).
Therefore, one must investigate [the meaning of] collecting the bowl, washing the feet, and spreading the mat right here; only then will it be possible."
According to this sutra, taking non-characteristic (*animitta*) as its central tenet, former commentators have matched the four lines on "non-self" (*anātman*) with the four-line verse.
This first chapter begins: "Thus have I heard. This is the characteristic of self (*ātman*). "Begging for food in the city" is the characteristic of person (*pudgala*).
"A great assembly of bhikṣus" is the characteristic of sentient beings (*sattva*). To say "Buddha" and "World-Honored One" is... [the characteristic of the Tathāgata].
This is the mark of a self-entity (*jīva*). One should not cling to such things in this way. I said:

"These various marks should all be returned to their original places and then swept away; if one does not lift up either the ground or the person, one falls into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*)."
If one raises [the dust] but does not sweep it away, one falls into the view of permanence (*sāśvatadṛṣṭi*). I have previously written a preface for the detailed commentary by Lin Renxian, stating:
"The absence of the mark of self (*ātman*) does not mean there is no self; the absence of the mark of person (*pudgala*) does not mean there is no person;

the absence of the marks of sentient beings (*sattva*) and life-span (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) does not mean there are no sentient beings or life-spans. One must not [conceive of them] by means of the body..."
Those who are able to see the Tathāgata do not lack a body. Those who practice giving without dwelling on signs do not lack the act of giving.
That there is no fixed dharma to be taught does not mean there is no dharma.
That the past, future, and present mind cannot be apprehended does not mean there is no mind. To have no place of abiding does not mean there is no abiding.
All [teachings] proceed from having speech to non-speech; for indeed, not being attached to existence is itself non-existence. Bodhidharma said, "Vast emptiness—there is no sage.
Emperor Wu of Liang did not understand this, so he asked, "Who is it that stands before me?
Had he realized this meaning, the thirty-two marks of a Buddha would have all dissolved within the act of spreading his seat and sitting upon it.
Chapter Two: The Section on the Request of Subhūti.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;

he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is marvelous, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata so skillfully protects and sustains all [bodhisattvas]..."
"Bodhisattva. He is well-entrusted to all bodhisattvas.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Subhūti; this means "Well-Auspicious," "Well-Manifested," or "Empty-Born. Regarding this, the Venerable Master Yun'an Liaoxing said:
"Subhūti is possessed by every person. If a person suddenly realizes the nature of emptiness and stillness, they are so named."

He understands emptiness; the nature of total emptiness is truly Bodhi, and thus he is named Subhūti. Since the nature of emptiness gives rise to the myriad dharmas, he is named Kūṭadanta (Empty-Born).
Since the nature of emptiness manifests in response to conditions to benefit people and things, he is also named Śubhavyūha (Good Manifestation).

Since his myriad practices are auspicious, he is also named Śubhakīrti (Good Fortune). As for the term "exposing one shoulder," in this land it signifies expressing regret and requesting absolution for one's offenses.

Thus, one bares the shoulder; in the Western lands, this is the ritual for generating reverence. Thus, one bares the shoulder. Regarding the "right shoulder," it is for the sake of convenience in action.

Regarding the "right knee," it is because the Buddha-dharma honors the right. "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) is a title for the Buddha. Subhūti, opening his speech, immediately praised [the teaching] as rare. What understanding did he have?
It was like a prince of the Golden Wheel who, in a single day, abandoned the royal palace to enter the snow mountains.
"Mountains! This matter is most rare. Disciples follow like clouds, begging for food according to conditions without stirring their emotions;

The notion of "self" is a critical cave. Because there is a self, one holds oneself as honorable and others as base.

It is thus transformed. Therefore, the mark of self (*ātman*) is the root of the disease of the four marks.

The *Mowang* says: "Ghosts and spirits possess nature but lack destiny; plants and trees possess destiny but lack nature;

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he would not be called a bodhisattva. Why is that?
The Tathāgata has said: "That which is called the adornment of Buddha-fields is in fact no adornment; it is merely named 'adornment.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata says that he is truly a bodhisattva."
The Buddha taught that all dharmas are devoid of the marks of self, person, and so forth. Since these dharmas are fundamentally without self, how could there be even a trace of self?
To adorn a buddha-field is for the mind to possess subject and object; it is an obstruction.

In all such cases, one has not yet attained penetration into non-self and dharmas. The *Yao* (Excerpts) states: "A buddha-field is the field of the mind. By means of the jewels of concentration and wisdom..."
One who adorns the buddha-field within the mind is a bodhisattva; they do not speak of their own merit, and no one perceives their traces.
One who adorns the worldly buddha-field with jewels such as gold and pearls is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana);
they speak of their own merit and are constantly anxious for others to see them. The *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra* says: "For the sake of all sentient beings, [one] generates..."
The mind of great adornment is precisely that which does not perceive the marks of adornment.

Regarding "selflessness and dharmalessness," this refers to the two kinds of selflessness mentioned in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: namely, the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Selflessness of persons means that persons have no intrinsic essence; they arise due to karma. Selflessness of phenomena means that phenomena have no intrinsic essence.
It is established based on causes and conditions. If one performs the karma of wealth and nobility, one is born among the wealthy and noble;
if one performs the karma of poverty and lowliness, one is born among the poor and lowly. This person fundamentally has no inherent substance. It is like when one intends to cross a body of water.
Thus, for those who wish to travel by water, there is the method of boats and oars; for those who wish to travel by land, there is the method of carts and carriages.

These methods have no inherent substance. Mazu said: "The self-nature is originally complete in itself. Only when one does not become obstructed by matters of good and evil can one be called a practitioner of the Way.
To take what is good and reject what is evil, or to contemplate emptiness and enter meditative concentration—all these belong to the realm of conditioned fabrication."
A single thought of deluded imagination is the very root of birth and death within the triple world. To simply have no such thought is to eliminate the root of birth and death;
one immediately attains the supreme, precious jewel of the Dharma King. Therefore, it is said that such a person is truly a Bodhisattva.
Zhuangzi said: "The Yellow Emperor lost his pearl; only Xiangwang found it.
If there were a dharma by which one could attain bodhi, that would be to fixate upon form within the formless. Therefore, only non-attainment constitutes true attainment.
Thus Laozi said: "Those who lose are like those who have not lost; for those who are like those who have not lost, even their loss is joyful in its attainment. To know this is true understanding.
To lose it is to gain it; one gains it forever. ○ Chapter Eighteen:

Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? “It is so, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata possesses [the fleshly eye].”

“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.

"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye."
Within these seventeen sections, that which is called a "bodhisattva" is also like this; it is said that a bodhisattva should train in accordance with the Tathāgata.

Therefore, each section speaks of matters pertaining to the Tathāgata’s portion. Thus, O World-Honored One, even if one were to praise them to the utmost, one could not add so much as a hair’s breadth beyond what is here.
All five eyes are likewise manifested through such transformations.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Because the fleshly eye sees all forms; because the divine eye sees the minds of all sentient beings;
because the wisdom eye sees the faculties and spheres of all sentient beings; because the dharma eye sees all phenomena as they truly are;
and because the Buddha-eye sees the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. These are what the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* refer to as the five purified eyes.
The eye is it. All ordinary beings possess the five eyes, yet they are shrouded by a deluded mind and thus cannot see for themselves.
If there were no deluded mind or false thoughts, then the cataracts and obstructions would recede and vanish, the five eyes would open and become clear, and one would see all forms.
A monk asked a venerable elder: "Does the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara employ so many hands and eyes?"
"What? An elder said, "The whole body is hands and eyes. Yet, if one were to try to open even a single eye here, there would be none.
Subhūti, what do you think? As for all the sands in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say they are sand? Thus it was said.
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata has spoken of these as grains of sand. "Subhūti, what do you think?

Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and each of those Ganges Rivers had as many grains of sand as their own number—would the worlds of the Buddhas thus be many? "Very many, World-Honored One."
When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he frequently used the Ganges River as a metaphor.

The phrase "as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand" means that for each single grain of sand, there is a corresponding Ganges River. As for "Buddha-worlds," this refers to a world of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
since a Buddha must invariably appear to establish transformation within each such world, all worlds of ordinary beings are called Buddha-worlds. Huangbo said:
The Buddha said that this is sand. When the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, and various devas walk upon it, the sand does not rejoice.
When cattle, sheep, and ants trample it, the sand does not feel anger. Even when precious jewels and fragrant scents are placed upon it, the sand does not feel greed.
The stench of excrement and mud; even the sand is not foul. This mind is the mind that is no-mind. Sentient beings and Buddhas are further without distinction.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Within all those lands, whatever sentient beings there may be, with their various kinds of minds, the Tathāgata [knows them all]."
He knows them all. Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all minds are non-minds; it is precisely for this reason they are called "minds.
The Tathāgata fully knows these various kinds of mind. When such a mind gives rise to a thought, it immediately belongs to the root of delusion.
From the perspective of a Buddha, however, it possesses form and characteristics. Because it possesses form and characteristics, it can be known. If it were quiescent...

However, as for empty space, there is nothing that can be known of it. Furthermore, what is called the supernormal power of knowing others' minds refers to the fact that once another has given rise to a thought, it can be known.
Formerly, there was a person who held a chess piece in his hand.
When one who possesses the supernormal power of knowing others' minds observes it, they know it to be a chess piece because they themselves know it to be a chess piece.
However, they do not know the exact number of pieces; even if asked by another to state that number, they would still not know it, because they themselves do not know the number.
As for a Buddha, how could he possess only the supernormal power of knowing others' minds?
And that is all. Thus, when immeasurable sentient beings give rise to a single thought, [the Buddha] knows them all. The deluded mind is itself no-mind;
even the awakening to the deluded mind is likewise no-mind. Fundamentally there are no delusive thoughts, and the non-arising of the deluded mind is the original mind of self-nature.
Therefore, it is said: "This is called the mind."
Why is this? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended;
the future mind cannot be apprehended.
The mind and its faculties interact and fluctuate according to circumstances; thus, there are the three periods of time.
If one awakens to the truly singular mind, then there is no past, present, or future. If there were a past mind that could be extinguished, it would be extinguishing itself;
if there were a future mind that could arise, it would be arising itself. Since there would then be arising and extinguishing, it would not be eternal.
The true mind immediately gives rise to sixty-two kinds of false views and nine hundred kinds of afflictions.
The three minds of past, future, and present are all unobtainable; this very state is what is called "non-mind," yet it is also what is named "mind.
The mind that cultivates various states of mind belongs to the delusory; the non-mind that is the mind belongs to the real. As for the mind that acts as the mind...
The merging of the real and the false is precisely the Middle Way. The Second Patriarch said, "I have searched for the mind, but it is utterly unattainable.
The First Patriarch said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. This very mind that seeks is itself the mind that is utterly unattainable.
To grant peace to the mind—is this not precisely what is called "mind"? Thus, one can understand the meaning of the mind.
Long ago, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī saw a man who said, "I have committed the karma of killing; I shall certainly fall into hell."
"How shall you be saved? The Bodhisattva instructed him to go and see the Buddha. The Buddha asked: "You have committed an act of killing;
from what state of mind did it arise? Was it from the past, the future, or the present?
If it arose from a past mind, the past has already ceased. If it arose from a future mind, the future has not yet arisen. If it arose from the present..."
That which exists in the mind does not abide in the present, for the three minds cannot be apprehended simultaneously. Thus, there is no arising or activity.
Since there is no arising or activity, what can be seen regarding the characteristics of sin? The self-nature of the mind is the nature of all phenomena;
the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena is the true nature. You should not give rise to groundless fear. This person...
Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, he immediately realized that the nature of karmic offenses is empty and was no longer struck with fear.
Layman Luo asked Yantou, "What is it like when arising and ceasing never cease? Yantou rebuked him, saying, "Who is it that arises and ceases?
Tiantong’s verse says: "In this flurry of arising and ceasing, what is it? The past, the future, and the present."
All are formed by the arising and ceasing of the mind. Once one recognizes who it is that arises and ceases, the mind immediately becomes empty and the objective realm becomes still.

The two characters "condition" (yin) and "cause" (yuan) are the eyes; these [first] twenty sections constitute the cause of Buddhahood, while the subsequent twenty sections concerning the various marks of the form-body (rūpakāya) constitute the fruit of Buddhahood.

To clarify this:

Why is this? It is like a poor person who grasps gold and turns it into earth, while a wealthy person grasps earth and turns it into gold;

Section Twenty: Parting from Form and Parting from Characteristics.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of a body of perfect form? No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of a body of perfect form. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that a "body of perfect form" is [merely] a body of perfect form.
It is not the perfection of the physical body; it is called the perfection of the physical body. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the perfection of the various marks? "No, World-Honored One.

The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection of the various marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that the perfection of the various marks is not a perfection; it is called the perfection of the various marks."
The perfection of the marks is the cause of the merit of nineteen parts; it is signlessness (*animitta*). The perfection of the twenty-eight [features] is the fruit of signlessness.
It is the perfection of the thirty-two marks of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), and the perfection of all the eighty minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). — *Dànjīng* (Platform Sutra)
It is said: "Skin and flesh constitute the physical body (*rūpakāya*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The physical body is not the Buddha.

Observing this, one knows that the fleshly body contains no Tathāgata; yet one fails to realize that the True Tathāgata exists therein. One knows that the physical body is not the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
yet one fails to realize that the wondrous form-body (*vimalarūpakāya*) exists therein. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The pure and wondrous form-body."
It is manifested through the power of spiritual efficacy (*ṛddhi-bala*), which is called the "Body of Wondrous Form" (*rūpakāya*).
This is precisely the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies; it is the Dharma-body itself. It is not that there is a separate spiritual power used to manifest the Dharma-body.

For ordinary people, when told that all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are unattainable, they fear becoming attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is said: "In contemplating emptiness, one does not fail to see form; in seeing form, everything is none other than empty."
Then one falls into the error of arid desolation. Little do they realize that emptiness and form are one and the same, and existence and non-existence are no different.
If one can perceive all bodies within the bodiless and perceive all marks within the markless, then as for the physical body and its various marks—
How could there ever be any deficiency? To be fully endowed with all marks is precisely the intention of abiding in the marks;
to be fully endowed with all marks is itself the functioning of the markless self.
The Layman Dongpo said: "Sentient beings are stubborn, fierce, and self-willed; they refuse to believe and enter [the Way].
Therefore, all the worthy sages remain hidden and do not appear. Only at Mount Emei, Wutai, Lu Shan, and Tiantai do extraordinary manifestations and transformations still emerge.
This is because their compassion is profound and deep, and they are urgent in reaching out to sentient beings; they manifest fully endowed with all marks."
It is likewise. Thus, there is a verse which says: "May one understand these characteristics. Who is it that binds you?

That which is complete in all characteristics is the point where one is urgently engaged with things; that which is not complete is the point where one is liberated from the bonds of characteristics."
The Record of the Hall of Great Compassion states: "If one pulls a single hair, the head moves;
if one plucks a single pore, the body reacts. Thus, all hairs are my head, and all pores are my body.
Yet, although they are all my head, they cannot perform the functions of the head; and although they are all my body, they cannot possess the capacities of the body.
If there were wisdom, then things would have something to disturb it. It is further said: "Without a body, there is no means to manifest the multitude of thousands of millions of bodies;
without thousands of millions of bodies, there is no means to demonstrate the ultimate state of mindlessness."

Do not have such a thought. Why is this? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma, they slander the Buddha; they do not understand.
Subhūti, it is because of what I have said: one who preaches the Dharma has no dharma whatsoever to preach; this is called preaching the Dharma.
As stated previously, there is no fixed dharma to be preached; rather, one speaks according to what is appropriate, yet that which is spoken is in all cases ungraspable.
This is still a form of discourse. Reaching this point, it is thoroughly swept away, and one simply says:

"There is no dharma that can be taught. Do not harbor such thoughts; this is stated with finality. Not only is there no teaching, but there is also no thought thereof. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:

If one does not speak of all dharmas, then the work of transformation and instruction will be ruined; thus, one knows that there is "no speaking. This is not a matter of remaining silent out of stubbornness;
rather, one speaks with a mind that abides nowhere. Such speech pervades the world without the fault of contradicting the Dharma.
Yan said: "Though I eat all day long, I have never eaten a single grain of rice; though I wear clothes all day long, I have never worn a single thread."
Once there was a single strand of silk hanging [there]. For this reason, our Buddha spoke crosswise and spoke straight for forty-nine years, yet he never uttered a single word.
If one says that the Tathāgata has preached any Dharma, one will be unable to understand what I have said.
Even if one could cause heavenly flowers to fall in profusion, it would still be the second best; only being able to sit [in meditation] [is the true state].
Severing the ten directions and forging them into a single whole is beyond the reach of words; this is what is called the true teaching of the Dharma.
Confucius said, "I wish to remain without words. Laozi said, "He who knows does not speak. One must understand that the state of no-speech and non-speaking is precisely why there is speaking;
thus one will know that the state of no-explanation is precisely why there is explaining.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being preached, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings. Why is this?
Subhūti, as for 'sentient beings, sentient beings,' the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; it is merely a designation."
Regarding "sentient beings" and "the life of wisdom": Subhūti has thoroughly realized the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom and entered the profound gate of awakening. His wisdom awakens to non-arising;

he perceives the life of the original source as neither departing nor arriving. Therefore, it is called the "life of wisdom. If one gives rise to the mind of faith, one then becomes attached to the view of a Buddha. Thus...
To say "not a sentient being" leads to a lack of faith, which results in clinging to the views of ordinary worldlings; therefore, it is said "not not a sentient being.
These two views must both be swept away so that the holy and the ordinary are equally exhausted, with no separation between the two realms.
Thus it is said: "Sentient beings, sentient beings—what the Tathāgata calls 'sentient beings' are not sentient beings; they are merely named 'sentient beings.'"
Someone asked, "How is it that all sentient beings of the great earth together attain Buddhahood? Xiying said, "He sees that sentient beings are Buddhas;

The *Laozi* says: "If one sets aside sagehood and abandons wisdom, the people will benefit a hundredfold. It also says: "Always cause the people to be without knowledge and without desire.
Confucius said: "The people may be made to follow [the Way]. This is the original face of all sentient beings.

No Dharma Can Be Attained** Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."

Subhūti feared that although those who hear the Dharma have heard it repeatedly, they might still fail to attain realization and thus be unable to give rise to a mind of true faith;
or perhaps they might still claim that the Tathāgata has something to be attained regarding bodhi. Therefore, he asked again to resolve this and clarify the matter.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is; there is nothing further to be said. He then reiterated: "There is not even the slightest [attainment]."
The Dharma can be attained. This means that not only are the two dharmas of emptiness and existence unattainable, but even the Middle Way itself is unattainable.
Therefore, as this Dharma is explained, it is equal; the three truths are all perfectly complete.
Ānanda asked the Venerable Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden brocade *kāṣāya*, what else has the World-Honored One transmitted?

Chapter Twenty-Three: The Section on Purifying the Mind and Practicing Goodness Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal; it has no high or low.
This is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment). By means of non-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
Then one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, that which is called "wholesome dharmas" by the Tathāgata is not, in fact, wholesome dharmas;

Such is the fundamental substance (*dharmatā*): within the six realms of existence, the mind does not diminish;

Regarding things: when they are level, there is neither high nor low; when they are equal, there is neither heavy nor light. This may be called the ultimate goodness of the Dharma.
Nevertheless, since Buddhas and ordinary beings are identical in this single Dharma, how could there be such a thing as a "good Dharma" that Buddhas alone have specially attained?
Therefore it is said: "It is not a good Dharma. This follows from the previous statement that not even the slightest dharma can be attained. This...
To say that these dharmas are equal means that both attainment and non-attainment are altogether equal.

Therefore, what is called "wholesome dharmas" is not, in fact, wholesome dharmas.

Extinction. In reality, there is no such thing as the Tathāgata’s extinction.
